edition.note: Open Library lists only 2014 printings (HarperBusiness hardcover ISBN 9780062273208, 289 pp.; HarperCollins ebook; Blackstone audio, Mar 04, 2014); no revised or later edition found. Chapter numbers in the Lessons match the nine-chapter 2014 text.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Chapters 1 to 3: how Horowitz took Loudcloud from boom to near-death and rebuilt it as Opsware. It matters because any startup you co-found will hit its own crash.
rows.note: Secondary (chapter notes): chapters 1 "From Communist to Venture Capitalist", 2 "I will survive", 3 "This time with feeling" come before 4 "When things fall apart"; the Loudcloud/Opsware story is told in 1-3. Publisher table of contents could not be fetched (harpercollins.com blocked).

rows.claim: In 1999 Ben Horowitz co-founded Loudcloud with Marc Andreessen, Tim Howes and In Sik Rhee. It ran websites and software for customers on its own servers, an early form of cloud computing.
rows.note: "The formation of Loudcloud, Inc. was announced in September 1999"; cofounders named: Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, Tim Howes, Sik Rhee.

rows.claim: Loudcloud raised large sums in the dot-com boom, then the 2000 crash wiped out many of its customers. Private money dried up, so Horowitz chose to take the company public in 2001.
rows.note: $68 million venture financing by Feb 2000 plus "another $120 million" by mid-2000; "On March 9, 2001, Loudcloud held its initial public offering"; "investment climate for Internet-based companies was not favorable". Customers hit by the crash and no private investors: secondary summary of the book at https://www.shortform.com/blog/loudcloud/ ("With no investors offering to invest, Loudcloud had no other option").

rows.claim: The IPO was priced at $6 a share in a collapsing market, and the press mocked it. Still, it raised the cash that kept the company alive.
rows.note: "Loudcloud priced its shares at $6 and offered 25 million shares, raising $150 million". Press reaction: shortform.com/blog/loudcloud/ "The press pilloried them".

rows.claim: In 2002 he sold the Loudcloud services business and its customers to EDS. Loudcloud kept its automation software and renamed itself Opsware.
rows.note: June 2002: "sell its core managed services and hosting business to EDS for $63.5 million in cash"; "adopted the name Opsware, Inc. later in the year". Horowitz's own essay https://a16z.com/the-case-for-the-fat-startup/ agrees: "Loudcloud sells the managed services business to EDS ... changes its name to Opsware".

rows.claim: Opsware's stock fell as low as 35 cents a share, and the company came close to dying again. Horowitz kept going, one hard decision at a time.
rows.note: Horowitz in interview: "everyone who dumped our stock so it dropped to $0.35 a share". Secondary summary of the book (shortform.com/blog/opsware/): "fell to a low of $0.35 per share, representing a valuation of $30 million", after the EDS sale.

rows.claim: In 2007 Hewlett-Packard bought Opsware for about $1.6 billion. The company the press had written off became a famous software exit.
rows.note: SEC filing, agreement dated July 20, 2007: HP to acquire Opsware for "$14.25 per share, or approximately $1.6 billion".

rows.claim: For you, the Struggle may be a startup that misses its target. Keeping your 25x capital plan separate from the company means one failure cannot take both.
rows.note: No book claim to check: "25x capital plan" is the app's own financial-independence target applied to the reader, not a figure attributed to Horowitz. The Card does not present it as the book's. Left unchanged.

rows.claim: Horowitz's view of the one-on-one: it is the employee's meeting, not the manager's. The employee sets the agenda and does about 90 percent of the talking.
rows.note: Horowitz: "it is the employee's meeting rather than the manager's meeting"; "the employee should set the agenda"; "the manager should do 10% of the talking and 90% of the listening".

rows.claim: Programming your culture: small, unusual rules shape behaviour more than value statements. At Andreessen Horowitz, a partner late to a founder meeting pays $10 a minute.
rows.note: Horowitz: "a ruthlessly enforced $10/minute fine for being late to a meeting with an entrepreneur".
